## Where Did the Term White Magic Come From?


The idea of beneficial magic is older than the English phrase. Blessings, protective rites, divination, sacred speech, and healing customs appear across many societies. Those practices did not wait for one English label, and they should not be folded into it after the fact.


For the phrase itself, the[Oxford English Dictionary factsheet](https://www.oed.com/dictionary/white-magic_n) places its earliest recorded English evidence in 1614, in Walter Raleigh’s *The History of the World* . “Earliest recorded” matters here. It tells us what survives in the OED’s evidence, not the first moment anyone spoke the words.


Raleigh wrote “White Magicke” beside the Greek-derived term *theurgia* . In his account, it meant a supposed conference with good spirits or angels. He then rejected the practice in openly skeptical language. The[digitized 1614 volume](https://archive.org/details/historyofworld00rale) preserves a useful tension: the phrase already marked a claimed difference between helpful and harmful spirit work, while the person recording it did not accept the practitioners’ premise.


That tension belongs to the history of magic. The label on a practice has often depended on who held the pen, the pulpit, the court record, or the authority to decide what counted as religion and what counted as forbidden magic.


### The Renaissance was never a clean two-color map


Early modern Europe held several overlapping conversations about magic. Philosophers wrote about natural magic and the hidden properties of the world. Ceremonial practitioners worked with prayers, names, timing, and ritual forms. Community practices existed beside learned ones. Church and civic authorities judged some of them through their own theological and legal categories.


Historian Paola Zambelli’s[study of white and black magic in the European Renaissance](https://doi.org/10.1163/ej.9789004160989.i-282) follows the contact among learned magic, popular rites, ceremony, and witchcraft. That contact is a better guide to the period than a tidy shelf with “good” on one side and “evil” on the other.


The vocabulary kept changing. “White magic” grew beyond Raleigh’s narrow reference to theurgy and became a broader label for magic presented as helpful, protective, or morally permitted. By the twentieth century, occult writers, modern witches, and popular culture were using several inherited terms at once. Their meanings varied by community.


A history of white magic therefore has two tracks. One follows the phrase through books and public debate. The other follows living practices, many of which have their own names and histories. The tracks meet, but they are not interchangeable.
